weeks.theme: Intake openings, identity verification, and setting expectations

scenarios.title: Open the intake and confirm identity in a busy ED triage bay
scenarios.situation: You greet an adult patient and spouse at the triage desk during a rush hour. You must quickly establish rapport, confirm full name and date of birth, and explain what will happen next.
targetPhrases: Hi, I’m [Name], one of the nurses on triage today.
Can you tell me your full name and date of birth, please?
Let me make sure I pronounced your name correctly: [repeat name].
Here’s what will happen in the next few minutes.
I’ll ask a few quick questions to keep you safe.
If I speak too fast, please tell me and I’ll slow down.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse opens professionally, verifies two identifiers without error, and sets a clear 2–3 step expectation for the intake flow.

scenarios.title: Interpreter or communication accommodation setup
scenarios.situation: The patient’s daughter requests help because her father is hard of hearing. You need to arrange a communication aid and confirm understanding.
targetPhrases: Do you prefer written notes, an interpreter, or a video relay?
I will bring the device now so we can communicate clearly.
I’ll check back to make sure this works well for you.
Please let me know if you need me to repeat or rephrase.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse offers appropriate accommodations and confirms that the patient can follow along before proceeding.

scenarios.title: Privacy check and who can stay
scenarios.situation: Two family members want to stay during intake. You must confirm the patient’s preference and privacy boundaries.
targetPhrases: Who would you like to stay with you while we talk?
We’ll discuss personal health information now.
If you prefer, we can speak privately.
I’ll share updates only with the person you choose.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse obtains patient preference and politely enforces privacy boundaries.

weeks.theme: Chief complaint and symptom exploration with plain language

scenarios.title: Elicit the chief complaint efficiently
scenarios.situation: You have five minutes to understand why the patient came in and how urgent it is.
targetPhrases: What brought you in today?
When did this start? Has it gotten better, worse, or the same?
On a scale of 0 to 10, how would you rate your pain right now?
What makes it better or worse?
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse captures chief complaint, onset, severity, and modifiers concisely without medical jargon.

scenarios.title: Clarify red flags and rule-out questions
scenarios.situation: Patient reports chest discomfort. You must ask targeted safety questions before vitals.
targetPhrases: Is the pain crushing, tight, or sharp?
Do you feel short of breath, sweaty, or nauseated?
Does the pain spread to your arm, jaw, or back?
Have you had this before?
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse asks appropriate screening questions and flags urgency for rapid triage.

scenarios.title: Teach-back to confirm understanding
scenarios.situation: After summarizing what you heard, you ensure alignment before moving on.
targetPhrases: Let me repeat what I heard to make sure I got it right.
In your own words, what is your main concern today?
Did I miss anything important?
We’ll take your vitals next and update you on timing.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse uses teach-back to confirm shared understanding and next steps.

weeks.theme: Medical history, medications, and allergy verification

scenarios.title: Allergy verification with specific reactions
scenarios.situation: Patient says they are allergic to penicillin. You must clarify reaction and severity.
targetPhrases: What happens when you take penicillin?
Is it a rash, swelling, trouble breathing, or something else?
When did this last happen?
I’ll add that to your chart to keep you safe.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse documents substance and reaction accurately and communicates safety intent.

scenarios.title: Medication reconciliation including over-the-counter and herbal
scenarios.situation: Patient brings a bag of medicines. You need to list name, dose, frequency, and last dose taken.
targetPhrases: Let’s go through your medicines one by one.
What is the dose and how often do you take it?
When was your last dose?
Do you take any vitamins, herbs, or over-the-counter medicines?
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse captures complete med list with last dose and includes non-prescription items.

scenarios.title: Past history essentials for triage
scenarios.situation: You need key history items relevant to today’s visit without going off track.
targetPhrases: Any major surgeries or hospital stays?
Any heart, lung, or diabetes issues?
Are you pregnant or could you be?
I’ll focus on what matters for today’s visit.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse efficiently gathers high-yield history tied to presenting complaint.

weeks.theme: Administrative intake, consent, and privacy in plain language

scenarios.title: ID and insurance confirmation without jargon
scenarios.situation: You must verify insurance coverage and explain any forms while keeping clinical flow moving.
targetPhrases: May I verify your address and insurance on file?
This form allows us to treat you and bill your insurance.
Please sign here to show you understand and agree.
I can answer any questions before you sign.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse verifies admin details and explains forms clearly and politely.

scenarios.title: HIPAA-friendly update boundaries
scenarios.situation: A friend asks for details about the patient’s condition. You must protect privacy.
targetPhrases: I want to protect [Name]’s privacy.
I can share general information, but not details without permission.
Let me check who is listed as the contact person.
With [Name]’s okay, I can update you.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse maintains privacy while offering appropriate alternatives.

scenarios.title: Documenting consent conversation
scenarios.situation: After explaining a routine procedure, you document patient understanding and consent.
targetPhrases: We discussed what will happen, benefits, and possible risks in simple terms.
The patient had a chance to ask questions.
The patient agreed to proceed.
I documented consent in the chart.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse records a clear, compliant note of the consent discussion.

weeks.theme: Vitals, triage priority, and explaining wait times

scenarios.title: Explain vitals and purpose
scenarios.situation: A nervous patient resists having vitals taken. You need to reassure and proceed.
targetPhrases: I’ll check your temperature, blood pressure, pulse, and oxygen level.
This helps us see how your body is doing right now.
It takes just a minute and doesn’t hurt.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse reassures patient and completes vitals smoothly.

scenarios.title: Set expectations for triage and queueing
scenarios.situation: Lobby is full and waits are long. You must explain how triage works and expected timing.
targetPhrases: We see the sickest patients first, not just in arrival order.
Your safety is our priority; I’ll keep you updated.
Right now the estimated wait is about [X] minutes.
Please tell me right away if your symptoms change.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse explains triage fairness and gives a realistic time window.

scenarios.title: Escalate based on vitals or symptoms
scenarios.situation: You notice abnormal vitals. You must communicate urgency to the team and family calmly.
targetPhrases: I’m going to alert the provider now because of your numbers.
We’ll move you to a room for closer monitoring.
I’ll update your family as soon as we settle you.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse communicates urgency without causing panic and initiates escalation steps.

weeks.theme: Special populations and caregivers: pediatric and geriatric intakes

scenarios.title: Pediatric intake with caregiver present
scenarios.situation: You intake a 5-year-old with fever and a worried parent. You must address both child and caregiver.
targetPhrases: Hi [Child’s Name], I’m going to check your temperature.
To the parent: What was the highest temperature you saw at home?
Any medicines given today and what time?
I’ll explain everything we do before we do it.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse uses child-friendly language and collects accurate history from caregiver.

scenarios.title: Geriatric intake with possible confusion
scenarios.situation: An older adult seems disoriented. You must assess safely and involve the family contact.
targetPhrases: I’ll ask short questions one at a time.
Do you have a health care proxy or someone we can update?
I want to make sure you’re safe—have you fallen recently?
With your permission, I’ll update your [relationship].
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse adapts communication and confirms appropriate contact for updates.

scenarios.title: Mobility, fall risk, and assistive devices
scenarios.situation: Patient uses a cane and is unsteady. You need to document mobility and plan for safety.
targetPhrases: Do you use any devices like a cane, walker, or oxygen?
Have you fallen in the last 3 months?
I’ll help you stand and move safely.
I’ll add fall precautions to your chart.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse identifies fall risk and implements basic precautions.

weeks.theme: Explaining tests and procedures before they happen

scenarios.title: Prepare patient for lab work
scenarios.situation: You must explain what the blood tests are for and how long results may take.
targetPhrases: We’ll draw a small sample of blood from your arm.
These tests check things like infection and electrolytes.
Results usually take about [X] minutes.
I’ll update you as soon as we have them.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse explains purpose, process, and timing in plain language.

scenarios.title: Imaging prep with simple instructions
scenarios.situation: Patient is going for an X-ray/CT. You must explain removal of metal items and positioning.
targetPhrases: Please remove metal items like jewelry or belts.
You’ll need to lie still for a few minutes.
If you feel uncomfortable, tell the tech right away.
We’ll bring you back here after the test.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse delivers clear, actionable prep steps and reassures patient.

scenarios.title: NPO/fasting clarification
scenarios.situation: Pre-procedure fasting is required. You must ensure the patient understands what is and isn’t allowed.
targetPhrases: Nothing to eat or drink means no food, gum, or water.
You can take essential medicines with a small sip if the doctor says it’s okay.
Fasting helps keep you safe during the procedure.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse communicates NPO instructions clearly and confirms understanding.

weeks.theme: Managing delays and proactive family updates

scenarios.title: Update family about delays and new ETA
scenarios.situation: A test is delayed by 90 minutes. Family is anxious. You must provide a calm update and revised plan.
targetPhrases: Thank you for your patience; I have an update.
The test is delayed about 90 minutes due to high volume.
Here’s what we can do in the meantime.
I’ll check back with you by [time].
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse acknowledges feelings, states reason, offers options, and gives a time-bound follow-up.

scenarios.title: Waiting room rounds: quick touchpoints
scenarios.situation: You perform quick rounds to prevent frustration. You must deliver 30–60 second updates.
targetPhrases: I wanted to check in with you.
No new results yet, but you are still in the queue.
Please let me know if anything changes.
I’ll return in about [X] minutes.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse reduces uncertainty with concise, regular updates.

scenarios.title: Escalate concerns to charge nurse
scenarios.situation: Family reports worsening symptoms during a delay. You must escalate and keep them informed.
targetPhrases: Thank you for telling me right away.
I’m notifying the charge nurse now.
We’re moving you up due to the change in symptoms.
I’ll stay with you until we’re set.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse appropriately escalates and communicates rationale to family.

weeks.theme: Handoffs and concise documentation of intake

scenarios.title: SBAR handoff to provider after intake
scenarios.situation: You summarize a new arrival to the PA/MD using SBAR.
targetPhrases: Situation: [Name], [age], here for [chief complaint].
Background: key history and meds.
Assessment: vitals and main findings.
Recommendation: next steps needed now.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse delivers a 30–60 second SBAR with only relevant details.

scenarios.title: Charting a clear intake note
scenarios.situation: You write a concise note that another nurse can act on without clarification.
targetPhrases: Chief complaint in patient’s words: "…"
Allergies with reactions: …
Meds with last dose: …
Plan and patient education: …
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse produces a structured note that meets unit standards and is easy to follow.

scenarios.title: Correcting documentation errors
scenarios.situation: You notice a mistake in the chart. You must correct it properly.
targetPhrases: I’m adding a late entry to correct…
Entered in error—see corrected note.
Maintaining accurate records keeps you safe.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse amends documentation following policy and explains why accuracy matters.

weeks.theme: In-person family updates after triage or tests

scenarios.title: Post-triage status update
scenarios.situation: You inform family about room placement and initial plan.
targetPhrases: Thank you for waiting. Here’s where we are now.
[Name] is moving to Room [#] for closer monitoring.
Next, the provider will examine them within about [X] minutes.
I’ll stay your point of contact for updates.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse gives clear status, next steps, and timeframe with a single point of contact.

scenarios.title: Explaining what has been ruled out or still pending
scenarios.situation: Family asks, "What do you know so far?" You must avoid speculation and be clear.
targetPhrases: So far, we have ruled out [X].
We are still waiting on [tests/results].
I can’t speak to diagnosis, but I can share the plan and timing.
I’ll update you as soon as results come in.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse communicates boundaries while keeping the family informed.

scenarios.title: Setting visiting expectations and boundaries
scenarios.situation: Multiple relatives want to enter at once. You must set limits kindly.
targetPhrases: For safety, only two visitors at a time.
Let’s rotate so everyone gets a chance.
Please keep phones on silent and the walkway clear.
Thank you for helping us care for [Name].
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse enforces visiting rules respectfully and consistently.

weeks.theme: Phone updates: identity verification, voicemails, and callbacks

scenarios.title: Verify identity before sharing information
scenarios.situation: You call the listed contact to provide an update and must confirm identity before sharing.
targetPhrases: Before I share an update, can you confirm your full name and relationship to [Name]?
Please verify [DOB/address] for privacy.
Thank you. Here’s the update…
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse verifies identity per policy before providing any details.

scenarios.title: Professional voicemail that prompts action
scenarios.situation: You must leave a HIPAA-safe voicemail that leads to a timely callback.
targetPhrases: Hello, this is Nurse [Name] from [Unit].
This is a non-urgent update for [First Name only].
Please call us back at [number] and reference [case/unit].
We’re available until [time].
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse leaves a clear, privacy-safe message with callback details.

scenarios.title: Handling a worried caller with empathy and structure
scenarios.situation: A family member is very anxious on the phone. You must calm them and share what you can.
targetPhrases: I hear that you’re worried, and that’s understandable.
Here’s what I can share right now…
Next steps are… and the expected timing is…
I’ll call you by [time] with an update or sooner if anything changes.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse acknowledges emotion, shares allowed info, and commits to a time-bound follow-up.

weeks.theme: Sharing difficult updates within nursing scope

scenarios.title: Minor complication or setback
scenarios.situation: A routine IV failed and needs to be restarted. Family is frustrated. You must explain and reset expectations.
targetPhrases: I want to be transparent about what happened.
The IV stopped working; we need to place a new one.
This can happen, and we’ll minimize discomfort.
We expect this to take about [X] minutes.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse explains clearly, accepts responsibility, and outlines the fix and timeline.

scenarios.title: Delays due to abnormal labs
scenarios.situation: Labs show an issue requiring more tests. You must update without diagnosing.
targetPhrases: Some results need a closer look, so we’re ordering additional tests.
The provider will explain the details.
Right now, here’s what we’re doing to keep [Name] safe…
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse shares implications and next steps without overstepping scope.

scenarios.title: When to pause and involve the provider
scenarios.situation: Family asks for prognosis. You must recognize scope limits and bring in the provider.
targetPhrases: That’s an important question for the provider to answer.
Let me bring them in so you get the full picture.
I’ll stay with you while we talk together.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse redirects appropriately and facilitates a warm handoff.

weeks.theme: Working with interpreters and multi-party updates

scenarios.title: On-demand interpreter for an in-person update
scenarios.situation: Family prefers another language. You must set up a professional interpreter and run a brief update.
targetPhrases: I’ll bring a certified interpreter to avoid misunderstandings.
Please speak in short phrases and pause for interpretation.
I’ll confirm understanding with teach-back.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse uses interpreter effectively and confirms comprehension.

scenarios.title: Three-way phone update with remote family member
scenarios.situation: You conference in an out-of-state relative for a status update.
targetPhrases: I’m adding [Name] to the call now.
Let’s confirm who is authorized to receive updates.
I’ll summarize next steps for everyone before we end.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse manages turn-taking, privacy, and a shared summary of next steps.

scenarios.title: Documenting interpreter use
scenarios.situation: After the conversation, you must document interpreter details.
targetPhrases: Interpreter ID/Name and language: …
Mode: in-person/video/phone.
Patient/family teach-back confirmed.
Note entered at [time].
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse completes compliant documentation of interpreter involvement.

weeks.theme: De-escalation and service recovery for families

scenarios.title: Family upset after being transferred multiple times
scenarios.situation: A relative says they’ve been transferred three times and no one has answers. You must de-escalate and take ownership of the next step.
targetPhrases: I’m sorry you’ve had to repeat yourselves; that’s frustrating.
I will own your update from here.
In the next 10 minutes, I will get you an answer or a timeline.
Here’s my name and the unit phone number.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse validates feelings, takes ownership, and sets a concrete follow-up commitment.

scenarios.title: Setting boundaries with aggressive tone
scenarios.situation: A family member raises their voice at the desk. You must keep everyone safe and de-escalate.
targetPhrases: I want to help, and I need a calm tone to do that.
Let’s step aside to talk privately.
If you prefer, I can bring the charge nurse now.
Here’s what I can do for you right away…
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse maintains safety, resets tone, and offers options.

scenarios.title: Service recovery after a missed update
scenarios.situation: A promised callback was delayed. You must apologize and reset trust.
targetPhrases: I apologize for the delay in getting back to you.
Here’s the information you were waiting for.
This is how I’ll prevent this from happening again.
Thank you for your patience.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse delivers a sincere apology, provides the missing info, and states a prevention step.

weeks.theme: Sensitive topics and end-of-life boundaries for nurses

scenarios.title: Visitor limits and quiet hours near end-of-life
scenarios.situation: Patient is near end-of-life. You must balance compassion with unit policy.
targetPhrases: We want to support your time together.
For safety, we can allow [X] visitors at a time; we’ll help rotate.
Please let us know cultural or spiritual needs so we can support them.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse shows compassion while applying policy and inviting support services.

scenarios.title: Involving chaplain or social work
scenarios.situation: Family needs additional support. You must offer and arrange services.
targetPhrases: Would you like me to call the chaplain or social worker?
They can help with resources and support.
I can stay with you until they arrive.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse offers appropriate resources and follows through promptly.

scenarios.title: What nurses can and cannot say about prognosis
scenarios.situation: Family asks, “How long do we have?” You must respond within scope and connect them to the provider.
targetPhrases: I understand why you’re asking.
That’s a question the provider needs to answer.
Let me bring them now so you get accurate information.
I’ll remain here with you.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse stays within scope and ensures a warm provider handoff.

weeks.theme: Capstone simulations: full intake to family update

scenarios.title: End-to-end intake under time pressure
scenarios.situation: Simulated ED arrival: complete identity check, chief complaint, vitals, safety screens, and SBAR handoff in under 8 minutes.
targetPhrases: Opening and identifiers completed.
Chief complaint summarized in patient’s words.
Allergies and meds with last dose captured.
SBAR delivered with clear recommendation.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse completes a safe, complete intake within time and communicates next steps to team.

scenarios.title: Proactive family update during a delay
scenarios.situation: Test backlog causes a 60-minute delay. Provide an in-person or phone update with a firm check-back time.
targetPhrases: Reason for delay explained in plain language.
Specific ETA and check-back time given.
Options offered for comfort and questions invited.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse reduces anxiety with a clear, time-bound update and options.

scenarios.title: Documentation audit and improvement
scenarios.situation: You review your chart for accuracy, clarity, and policy compliance, then rewrite one section for improvement.
targetPhrases: Identify one unclear or missing element.
Revise with concrete, plain-language phrasing.
Record interpreter or consent details if applicable.
Finalize with date/time stamp and signature.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Nurse demonstrates measurable improvement in clarity and compliance of documentation.

weeks.theme: Optional: Skill refresh or buffer week (use if holidays/staffing impact)

scenarios.title: Targeted review based on QA findings
scenarios.situation: Focus drills on the two weakest skills identified mid-program (e.g., teach-back, voicemail scripting).
targetPhrases: We’ll practice the exact lines that caused confusion.
Repeat, refine, and record for self-review.
Apply the checklist to reach consistency.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Team closes specific gaps with repeated, high-yield practice.

scenarios.title: Peer coaching circles
scenarios.situation: Small groups swap scripts and role-play tricky updates, giving structured feedback.
targetPhrases: One thing that worked was…
One suggestion for clarity is…
Let’s try that line again with simpler words.
scenarios.successLooksLike: Peers deliver actionable feedback and visible improvement within the session.

successCriteria.plainLanguage: Nurses complete a safe, complete intake without missing critical items and without confusing the patient or family.
successCriteria.measurableProxy: In simulation, 90% complete a standardized intake in under 8 minutes, correctly capturing identifiers, chief complaint, allergies with reactions, meds with last dose, and vitals; zero privacy breaches.

successCriteria.plainLanguage: Families feel informed and less anxious because updates are clear, time-bound, and empathetic.
successCriteria.measurableProxy: In role-plays, 90% deliver an update that includes reason, next step, ETA, and a promised check-back; include at least two empathy statements; teach-back used in 80% of cases.

successCriteria.plainLanguage: Documentation is clear enough that any covering nurse can act without follow-up questions.
successCriteria.measurableProxy: Chart audit shows a 25% reduction in omissions or unclear notes on a 10-point rubric; interpreter/consent documentation present in 95% of applicable cases.

kickoffMessage.en: Welcome to the 16-week English program for nurses focused on patient intake and family updates. We’ll practice real conversations you handle every shift: opening the intake, confirming identity, getting the story in plain language, setting expectations, giving proactive updates (in person and by phone), de-escalating tough moments, and documenting clearly. Expect two 60-minute sessions per week with short, repeated role-plays and feedback you can use on your next shift. Your voice matters—let’s make every intake safer and every update calmer.
kickoffMessage.ko: 환영합니다. 본 과정은 간호사를 위한 16주 영어 프로그램으로, 환자 접수와 보호자 안내에 초점을 둡니다. 매 근무 때 마주하는 실제 대화를 연습합니다: 접수 시작 인사, 본인 확인, 쉬운 영어로 증상 파악, 기대치 설정, 선제적 안내(대면 및 전화), 어려운 상황 완화, 그리고 명확한 기록까지. 주 2회 60분 수업으로 진행되며, 짧고 반복적인 역할극과 바로 써먹을 수 있는 피드백을 제공합니다. 여러분의 목소리가 중요합니다—더 안전한 접수와 더 차분한 안내를 함께 만들어 갑시다.
